strengths: Clearly motivated problem: Identifies genuine challenge of applying RL to dLLMs due to intractable log-likelihood and bias from using ELBO for negative rewards
Solid theoretical foundations: Theorem 1 provides valid EUBO based on Rényi variational bounds; Proposition 1 offers variance reduction analysis with detailed proofs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Four benchmarks, extensive ablations (Tables 2-13), robustness across inference strategies (Figure 6), and supplementary analyses (Pass@K, reward dynamics)
Consistent empirical improvements: Shows gains across all four tasks (3.6-27.0% at length 256), with detailed ablation studies supporting design choices
Thorough documentation: Complete implementation details, dataset specifications, reward functions, and qualitative examples facilitate reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core idea of using different bounds for positive/negative cases is straightforward; EUBO derived from well-established Rényi bounds; block-wise masking inspired by concurrent work; mixture approach is simple linear interpolation

Problematic hyperparameter selection: β values selected based on best test accuracy, raising generalization concerns; different β values required per task (1.0 for Sudoku, 1.5 for others, 2.0 for Countdown EUBO) indicates method requires careful calibration

Lacking statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; no validation that improvements are statistically meaningful; results appear to be single runs with only training dynamics reporting variance

Theoretical-practical gap: EUBO estimator acknowledged as biased but retained for tightness; mixture approach introduced as pragmatic fix for computational constraints rather than principled contribution; Proposition 1 analyzes variance but doesn't establish connection to actual RL performance

Confounded experimental components: Cannot cleanly separate contributions of sandwich bounds, block-wise masking, and mixture approach; ablations incomplete (Table 2 removes entire negative loss rather than isolating bounds)

Modest improvements on half the benchmarks: Only 3.6% on GSM8K and 2.6% on MATH500 versus 18.4% on Countdown and 27.0% on Sudoku; no clear explanation for the dramatic variance; improvements could be within noise given lack of significance testing

Limited scope and generalization: Evaluation restricted to reasoning tasks only; no preference alignment or instruction-following tasks; Sudoku uses 3-shot (base model too weak for 0-shot) with modified dataset; unclear applicability to other decoding strategies beyond block-wise semi-autoregressive
Reproducibility concerns: Code not available; m=2 Monte Carlo samples extremely low; fixed ω=0.5 despite Figure 5e-f showing task sensitivity; hyperparameter selection procedure not fully specified

Incomplete analysis of design choices: Biased EUBO vs. unbiased bound (Table 10) suggests practical choice overrides theory; gradient dynamics (Figure 7) shown but causal link to performance unclear; p_mask=0.15 appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis

Missing critical comparisons: No ablation separating sandwich bounds from block-wise masking; no comparison to PPO-adapted baselines; limited discussion of when/why WD1 sometimes matches or exceeds SPG performance

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem: Identifies fundamental limitation of ELBO surrogates for handling negative rewards in dLLM RL
Solid theoretical contribution: Derives evidence upper bound (EUBO) via Rényi variational bound and proposes principled sandwiching approach
Strong, consistent experimental results: 3.6-27.0% improvements across four diverse benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, Countdown, Sudoku)
Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple strong baselines, extensive ablations on components and hyperparameters, robustness across inference strategies
Practical contributions: Block-wise masking strategy well-motivated with clear benefits (+23.9% on Countdown)
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed experimental setup, promised code release, transparent hyperparameters and few-shot examples
Thorough analysis: Proposition 1 on variance reduction, gradient dynamics (Figure 7), Pass@K analysis, and toy examples for intuition
Well-written and well-organized: Clear motivation, helpful visualizations, logical flow from problem to solution
weaknesses: Theoretical-practical gap: EUBO Monte Carlo estimate is biased (log outside expectation); mixture approach weakens theoretical guarantee that J_SPG ≤ J_group; implications under bias not rigorously analyzed
Severe Monte Carlo limitation: Only m=2 samples used due to computational constraints; risks high-variance estimates, especially with already-biased EUBO; no analysis of variance degradation

Pragmatic design choices limit generalizability: Mixture coefficient fixed at ω=0.5 despite per-coordinate optimal values existing; β requires task-specific tuning (1.0-2.0 range); reduces principled nature of approach
Limited experimental scope: Only one base model (LLaDA-8B) tested; Sudoku uses 3-shot while others 0-shot (confounding); no other dLLM architectures evaluated
Incomplete computational analysis: Claims similar runtime to baselines but provides no concrete timing comparisons; additional EUBO and mixture computations have unquantified overhead
Coordinate-wise gradient variance analysis: Proposition 1 analyzes variance per-coordinate but doesn't address multivariate correlations or properties in high dimensions
Model selection methodology: Uses test-set performance for tuning β (Section D.2), which is generally concerning despite final evaluation on held-out sets

Missing depth on bias-variance tradeoff: Table 10 shows loose unbiased bound performs worse, but doesn't investigate whether improvements from tighter biased bound reflect better approximation or implicit regularization

weaknesses: Limited core novelty: EUBO derivation straightforwardly applies known Rényi bounds; block-wise masking acknowledged as concurrent work; primarily combines existing techniques

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies a real flaw in applying ELBO to negative rewards, providing clear justification for the proposed approach
Solid theoretical framework: Derives tractable EUBO using Rényi variational bound with rigorous proofs (Theorems 1, Proposition 1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple benchmarks with extensive ablations, testing across diverse inference strategies and generation lengths
Strong empirical results: Substantial improvements on reasoning tasks (up to 27% on Sudoku) with consistent gains across benchmarks
Thorough documentation: Detailed appendix with hyperparameters, implementation details, and additional experiments supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Despite clean theoretical motivation, practical algorithm uses biased EUBO estimation, mixture approach (Eq. 8) lacks principled justification, and requires task-specific hyperparameter tuning (β ∈ {1.0, 1.5, 2.0})

Confounded contributions: Table 4 shows block-wise masking alone provides +23.9% improvement on Countdown—nearly as large as claimed improvements. Block-wise masking is orthogonal to the core contribution and specific to LLaDA's inference, complicating attribution of improvements

Problematic checkpoint selection: Selecting checkpoints based on test set performance introduces optimistic bias. Validation-based selection (Table 23) shows substantially smaller improvements, raising concerns about overfitting

Limited novelty: EUBO derivation is direct application of known Rényi bound (standard technique). The sandwiched objective idea—use lower bounds for maximization, upper bounds for minimization—is intuitive but not deeply novel
Narrow experimental scope: Tested only on LLaDA-8B without evaluation on other dLLM families. Limited to reasoning/coding tasks. Requires careful dataset-specific tuning, limiting generalizability

Incomplete theoretical justification: Mixture approach (Eq. 8) lacks formal motivation beyond empirical performance. Proposition 1 provides only per-coordinate variance analysis without full convergence guarantees. Acknowledged bias in EUBO estimation insufficiently addressed

Missing ablation studies: No thorough investigation of ELBO with increased Monte Carlo samples vs. mixture approach. Limited analysis of bound tightness in practice or why sandwiching fundamentally helps beyond lower-bound argument

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies genuine limitation in prior work—that ELBO-based RL for dLLMs cannot effectively learn from negative rewards, preventing use of relative/negative reward schemes

Sound theoretical contribution: Derives tractable Evidence Upper Bound (EUBO) using Rényi variational bounds; sandwich framework (LELBO ≤ log πθ ≤ LEUBO) is conceptually clean; Proposition 1 proves mixture approach reduces gradient variance

Comprehensive experimental validation: Six benchmarks across reasoning/coding tasks; consistent improvements (+3.6% to +27.0%); extensive ablations (Tables 3-4, 12-13) isolating each component; robustness across inference strategies (Figure 6)

Thorough technical execution: Block-wise masking well-motivated with empirical validation (Table 4: +23.9% gain); computational overhead minimal (Table 21); hyperparameter sensitivity analyzed; validation-based checkpoint selection provided (Table 23)
Strong reproducibility: Extensive implementation details, reward functions clearly specified, ablations on design choices (prompt masking, MC samples, fine-tuning), few-shot examples documented
Clear presentation: Intuitive figures explaining complex concepts (Figure 2, 8); problem formulation and solution strategy easy to follow despite technical depth
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: EUBO derivation relies entirely on standard Rényi variational bounds (not a new theoretical framework); block-wise masking acknowledged as concurrent work; mixture approach is heuristic interpolation lacking principled justification

Theory-practice gap: EUBO Monte Carlo estimation is biased due to Jensen's inequality (acknowledged but rationalized empirically); only m=2 samples used due to computational constraints (Table 20 hints m=4 helps but not pursued); no convergence guarantees or sample complexity analysis

Statistical rigor concerns: No confidence intervals, error bars, or multiple random seeds reported; unclear if results are from single runs; validation-based results in Table 23 but main results use test-set performance for checkpoint selection

Methodological gaps: No RL stabilization techniques (clipping, KL regularization, importance weighting) incorporated—acknowledged as open problem in Appendix F; off-policy bias from group-relative advantages not addressed in main work; fixed β and ω per-task rather than learned adaptively

Incomplete baseline comparisons: LLaDOU and UniGRPO both reimplemented without access to original code (faithfulness unverified); only 2/6 benchmarks evaluated against LLaDOU; computational cost explanation (7.5 vs 0.6 min) lacks detail on whether fundamental or implementation difference

Narrow scope: Evaluated only on LLaDA-8B-Instruct; block-wise masking specific to semi-autoregressive generation strategy; dLLMs remain niche compared to autoregressive LLMs; no multimodal or vision tasks; generalization to other architectures unclear
Modest gains on some tasks: +2.6% on MATH500 and +1.9% on HumanEval are meaningful but smaller than other benchmarks; no significance testing to establish statistical reliability

Presentation density: Critical content relegated to 28-page appendix; connection between EUBO bias and mixture efficacy underdeveloped in main text; notation mixing discrete/continuous time could be clearer
